prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. That is, groups of similar constructs were created and labelled and further specified, extended, split, or merged in the course of categorization until all constructs were assigned in satisfactory categories. For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. health, amenities & aesthetics This functional area addresses needs stated in rights related to sensory qualities of the environment, ad- dressing rights that deal with how a street should work to make people feel comfortable and secure (Los Angeles Walks, n.d.), as well as providing a healthy environment (Breines & Dean, 1974). This func- tional area also includes actions for placemaking and the provision of amenities for socializing, relaxing, rejuvenation (via adequate space, street furniture, vegetation, art, etc.). Along these lines, we can include building, planning, and design that provides human-scale , enclosure, memorability, transparency, etc. as discussed by Handy and Ewing in their study uncovering important urban design qualities for pedes- trians (Handy, Boarnet, Ewing, & Killingsworth, 2002). For example, the Los Angeles Walks’ Pedestrian Bill of Rights (Los Angeles Walks, n.d.), provides quite a few rights dealing with these sensory qualities, including appeal, safety and comfort, saying the people of Los Angeles have the right to: • Pedestrian-oriented building facades, trees, flower stands, trash cans, awnings, etc. • Safe and comfortable bus stops and public transit stations (also be a part of Access) • Appealing use of landscaping and available open space • Access to streets and buildings for disabled people • Clean surroundings, requiring removal of graffiti and advertisements from public property • Public works of Art Furthermore, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Pedestrian Bill of Rights (Breines & Dean, 1974) include many elements within this functional area, especially in the rights stating: • Urban residents shall have plentiful and generous open public places—outside of parks—for gatherings and ceremonies. • Pedestrians shall have the right to breathe clean air on streets, free of the harmful fumes of vehicles. • Standing room only on city streets shall end by providing benches for sitting and relaxation. • The sounds of human voices shall replace vehicular noise on city streets. 918 JOURNAL OF TRANSPORT AND LAND USE 14.1 • Urban man shall have the right to experience trees, plants, and flowers along city streets. • Cities shall exist for the care and culture of human beings, pedestrians all! Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s rights to the following align to this functional area (Appleyard et al., 1981): • The Street as a Livable, Healthy Environment • The Street as Neighborly Territory • The Street as a Place for Play and Learning • The Street as a Green and Pleasant Land 4.1.5 Access & connectivity This functional area addresses needs stated in rights related to land use accessibility, and accessible/ connected streets, buildings & networks for pedestrians, bicyclists and the those with disabilities. This includes larger scale land use and urban design activities that can have a meta-influence on a particular street section, including surrounding factors of land use, preservation, and street/network connection. This functional area also deals with the cognitive connectivity (wayfinding) and access to auto-alterna- tives, such as transit or micro-mobility options (bicycling networks). For example, Liga Peatonal’s state- ments of rights such as: • “A city that fits my needs” • “Adequate public transportation services” are both covered by this functional

As can be seen, the arterial road is negatively evaluated on Mental Comfort, Interaction and Environment. This does not surprise as on an arterial road, cyclists ride directly next to the motor traffic without any separation and usually with less space and distance from passing motor vehicles. Additionally, cyclists are surrounded by exhausts and noises from motor traffic. The Ease of Use is neither good Fig. 5. Average rating of the route attributes on each cluster. Negative values belong to a negative evaluation, positive values to a posi- tive evaluation. 257 F.L. Berghoefer and M. Vollrath T r a n s p o r t a t i o n R e s e a r c h P a r t F : P s y c h o l o g y a n d B e h a v i o u r 8 7 ( 2022)249–263 nor bad at arterial roads, and the Physical Comfort is evaluated slightly positive. Especially, the asphalt surface and the possibility to cycle fast might lead to a positive evaluation. On the other hand, arterial roads might be associated with traffic lights, which hinder the cycle flow, and might be the reason why the Physical Comfort is not rated very positively. Compared to an arterial road, the residential road has lower traffic speed and lower traffic volume. This leads to a slightly more positive evaluation in all the clusters compared to the arterial road, with the largest difference in Mental Comfort. Mental Comfort is evaluated as neither good nor bad, which means that a reduction in traffic speed and volume can reduce mental discomfort, while a missing cycling facility and less space for cyclists might prevent high Mental Comfort. The Physical Comfort also increases, probably due to the association with good surface, no obstacles, and no traffic lights. Furthermore, whereas ratings for Mental Comfort and Interaction are similar for most of the attributes, they diverge at the residential road, the bicycle boulevard, the shared space, and the park. These situations might be perceived as strenuous due to possible interaction with other road users, but due to lower traffic speed, less busy traffic, or less other road users stronger than the cyclist, they are still perceived as mentally comfortable. Interestingly, the evaluations of the different traffic volumes are more extreme than the associated road levels. That is, high traffic volume is similarly evaluated as arterial roads regarding Mental Comfort, Interaction, and Environment, but more negative regarding the Ease of Use and, in particular, Physical Comfort. Other vehicles might be associated as obstacles or hindrance of cycle flow, and the higher the traffic volume the lower the Physical Comfort. The evaluation of low traffic volume, on the other hand, is even more positive than the residential road, especially on Physical Comfort. prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):
{
"scores": {
"justice": {
"overall": 68.0,
"equity": 70.0,
"fairness": 60.0,
"accessibility": 75.0
},
"safety": 72.0,
"livability": 65.0,
"sustainability": 58.0,
"aesthetics": 80.0,
"comfort": 62.0,
"walkability": 70.0
},
"explanations": {
"justice": [
"Wide sidewalks and ramps improve accessibility",
"Lack of tactile paving reduces fairness for visually impaired users",
"Sidewalk width is suitable for wheelchairs, reflecting equitable distribution"
],
"safety": [
"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",
"Limited visible lighting may reduce nighttime safety",
"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],
"livability": [
"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],
"sustainability": [
"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],
"aesthetics": [
"Uniform building heights and consistent facade designs create visual coherence",
"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}
 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.
4. Do not mention RAG, retrieval, or prompt instructions in the explanations.

First, the elicited constructs were categorized in terms of content by two raters (A and B), similar to the method of the Inductive Category Formation by Mayring (2014). That is, groups of similar constructs were created and labelled and further specified, extended, split, or merged in the course of categorization until all constructs were assigned in satisfactory categories. For this categorization, only the constructs’ names were used, not the ratings. To validate the categories, the assignment of the constructs to the categories was repeated separately by rater A and a third rater C. These assignments were then compared to the first assignment to calculate the intrarater and the interrater reliability, respectively. The intrarater reliability described by Cohen’s Kappa gave κ =0.895 which is an “almost perfect” (Landis & Koch, 1977, p.165) agreement. This func- tional area also includes actions for placemaking and the provision of amenities for socializing, relaxing, rejuvenation (via adequate space, street furniture, vegetation, art, etc.). Along these lines, we can include building, planning, and design that provides human-scale , enclosure, memorability, transparency, etc. as discussed by Handy and Ewing in their study uncovering important urban design qualities for pedes- trians (Handy, Boarnet, Ewing, & Killingsworth, 2002). For example, the Los Angeles Walks’ Pedestrian Bill of Rights (Los Angeles Walks, n.d.), provides quite a few rights dealing with these sensory qualities, including appeal, safety and comfort, saying the people of Los Angeles have the right to: • Pedestrian-oriented building facades, trees, flower stands, trash cans, awnings, etc. • Safe and comfortable bus stops and public transit stations (also be a part of Access) • Appealing use of landscaping and available open space • Access to streets and buildings for disabled people • Clean surroundings, requiring removal of graffiti and advertisements from public property • Public works of Art Furthermore, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Pedestrian Bill of Rights (Breines & Dean, 1974) include many elements within this functional area, especially in the rights stating: • Urban residents shall have plentiful and generous open public places—outside of parks—for gatherings and ceremonies. • Pedestrians shall have the right to breathe clean air on streets, free of the harmful fumes of vehicles. • Standing room only on city streets shall end by providing benches for sitting and relaxation. • The sounds of human voices shall replace vehicular noise on city streets. 918 JOURNAL OF TRANSPORT AND LAND USE 14.1 • Urban man shall have the right to experience trees, plants, and flowers along city streets. • Cities shall exist for the care and culture of human beings, pedestrians all! Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s rights to the following align to this functional area (Appleyard et al., 1981): • The Street as a Livable, Healthy Environment • The Street as Neighborly Territory • The Street as a Place for Play and Learning • The Street as a Green and Pleasant Land 4.1.5 Access & connectivity This functional area addresses needs stated in rights related to land use accessibility, and accessible/ connected streets, buildings & networks for pedestrians, bicyclists and the those with disabilities. This includes larger scale land use and urban design activities that can have a meta-influence on a particular street section, including surrounding factors of land use, preservation, and street/network connection. This functional area also deals with the cognitive connectivity (wayfinding) and access to auto-alterna- tives, such as transit or micro-mobility options (bicycling networks). As can be seen, the arterial road is negatively evaluated on Mental Comfort, Interaction and Environment. This does not surprise as on an arterial road, cyclists ride directly next to the motor traffic without any separation and usually with less space and distance from passing motor vehicles. Additionally, cyclists are surrounded by exhausts and noises from motor traffic. The Ease of Use is neither good Fig. 5. Average rating of the route attributes on each cluster. Especially, the asphalt surface and the possibility to cycle fast might lead to a positive evaluation. On the other hand, arterial roads might be associated with traffic lights, which hinder the cycle flow, and might be the reason why the Physical Comfort is not rated very positively. Compared to an arterial road, the residential road has lower traffic speed and lower traffic volume. This leads to a slightly more positive evaluation in all the clusters compared to the arterial road, with the largest difference in Mental Comfort. Mental Comfort is evaluated as neither good nor bad, which means that a reduction in traffic speed and volume can reduce mental discomfort, while a missing cycling facility and less space for cyclists might prevent high Mental Comfort. The Physical Comfort also increases, probably due to the association with good surface, no obstacles, and no traffic lights. Furthermore, whereas ratings for Mental Comfort and Interaction are similar for most of the attributes, they diverge at the residential road, the bicycle boulevard, the shared space, and the park. These situations might be perceived as strenuous due to possible interaction with other road users, but due to lower traffic speed, less busy traffic, or less other road users stronger than the cyclist, they are still perceived as mentally comfortable. Interestingly, the evaluations of the different traffic volumes are more extreme than the associated road levels. That is, high traffic volume is similarly evaluated as arterial roads regarding Mental Comfort, Interaction, and Environment, but more negative regarding the Ease of Use and, in particular, Physical Comfort. Other vehicles might be associated as obstacles or hindrance of cycle flow, and the higher the traffic volume the lower the Physical Comfort. The evaluation of low traffic volume, on the other hand, is even more positive than the residential road, especially on Physical Comfort.
